title: engineering-stakes-quick-pitches-and-demo-hooks
body:
Purpose:
Short, tactical messaging + demo hooks targeted at three engineering personas: ML engineers, backend engineers, platform teams. This is a working note for SDRs, solutions engineers, and PMs to run quick experiments (A/B email, 2-screen demo, and a 1:1 technical deep dive).

TL;DR (one-liners):
- ML engineers: "Optimize token cost without changing model behavior — ship faster, test more prompts."
- Backend engineers: "Predictable latency and graceful degradation across traffic spikes — integrate like any other microservice."
- Platform teams: "Unified runtime and policies that let teams standardize inference across regions and clouds with auditability."

Persona profiles (one-sentence context each):
- ML engineer: cares about output fidelity, experiment velocity, local reproducibility, and evaluation guardrails. Often the owner of prompt/eval loops.
- Backend engineer: cares about stable 95th/99th latency, retries, idempotency, and cost predictability under load.
- Platform team: cares about multi-tenant isolation, quotas, private deployment, compliance, rollout policies, and runbooks.

What each persona actually fears (talktrack triggers):
- ML engineer fears: "my model changes behavior after deploy and I won't notice until it's in prod"; also worries about per-token cost when running large eval suites.
- Backend engineer fears: "the LLM endpoint will add tail latency and blow up our SLOs during peak"; also the operational burden of custom instrumentation.
- Platform team fears: "disparate teams spin up different endpoints and we lose visibility / control; legal will flag data exfiltration."

Core messages (by persona) — 30s / 2 min / demo hooks:
- ML engineers:
  - 30s: "Ship experiments faster: Redwood provides prefix caching, eval hooks, and rollbacks so you can iterate prompts without inflating token spend or surprise regressions."
  - 2min: Emphasize: built-in evals → regression alerts tied to your prompt sets; compare-before-after diffs; quantization profiles that keep logits intact; canary rollouts for model weights.
  - Demo hook: Live: run an eval suite (20 prompts) -> show cost and quality delta when switching quantization profile; trigger a regression alert and demonstrate automatic rollback.
  - KPI to call out: tokens per successful prompt, time-to-detect-regression, false-positive rate of alerts.

- Backend engineers:
  - 30s: "Treat LLM as any other backend service — SDKs, retries, circuit-breakers, and latency-aware routing with fallbacks to cheaper model variants."
  - 2min: Show deterministic SLO controls (latency tiers), explain request routing rules, and how caching avoids token costs while respecting strong consistency for user-specific context.
  - Demo hook: Backpressure simulation: replay a traffic spike and switch routing policy to degrade to shorter-context model; show 99th latency staying under target while throughput continues.
  - KPI to call out: P99 latency, tail-loss incidents avoided, percent of requests served by fallback.

- Platform teams:
  - 30s: "One control plane, consistent policies across hosted and private — central billing, audit logs, and per-team quotas."
  - 2min: Highlight VPC private deployment option, KMS integrations, per-route RBAC, and rollout/A/B feature gates that apply org-wide. Contrast with building and maintaining internal model-serving infra.
  - Demo hook: Show policy dashboard: create a per-team quota, set a canary rollout for a new model, and pull an audit log for a user request.
  - KPI to call out: time-to-provision-dedicated-capacity, mean-time-to-revoke-credentials, compliance‑audit readiness (logs retained).

Common objections and short rebuttals (copy-ready):
- "We host models ourselves." → "Great — Redwood can front your on-prem model with the same API and add batching, caching, and tracing without changing your model artifacts."
- "LLMs are too inconsistent for rollouts." → "We tie rollouts to prompt-based evals and can auto-fallback to validated model variants if regression thresholds are crossed."
- "Cost is unpredictable." → "We provide per-route token dashboards, batching suggestions, and quantization recommendations so you can forecast and enforce spend limits."

Competitive quick calls (scripting for SEs):
- Comp A (managed endpoint vendor): better for single-model serving but lacks built-in eval/regression hooks and org-level rollout policies. Script: "If you need simple hosting only, they fit; if you want inference governance, Redwood layers policies and regressions into the serving lifecycle."
- Comp B (open-source runtime): cheaper to start but long tail of ops. Script: "You can run it yourself — but Redwood reduces ops burden via managed kernels, autoscaling, and live regression detection."
- Comp C (LLM-API-first provider): broad model catalog but limited private deployment controls. Script: "They’re great for quick POCs; Redwood is for teams that need predictable economics and private deployment/compliance."

Suggested experiments / A-B tests (low-effort):
- Email A: ML engineers — subject: "Reduce token cost for eval suites by 30% (no prompt changes)"; CTA: run a 50-sample eval on us.
- Email B: Backend engineers — subject: "Keep P99 under X ms during traffic spikes"; CTA: we’ll replay 15min of your traffic and show routing policy impact.
- Landing copy test: emphasize metrics (tokens saved, p99 latency) vs. storytelling (customer use case).

Collateral ideas for each persona (quick list):
- ML engineers: notebook walkthrough (Jupyter) showing eval and rollback; prompt-regression cookbook; quantization tradeoff matrix.
- Backend engineers: sample middleware (Go/Node) for retries + routing; latency SLO playbook; step-by-step traffic replay guide.
- Platform teams: deployment checklist for VPC/on-prem; compliance one-pager (audit + KMS); policy-as-code examples.

Open questions / risks to validate with research:
- Which eval metrics resonate most with ML engineers (ROUGE vs. pragmatic task accuracy vs. human eval)?
- How much visibility into kernel-level optimizations do backend/platform teams want? Too much detail can be a blocker.
- Which competitor messages trigger procurement conversations vs. technical evaluation?

Next steps / to-dos (owner & timeline):
- Maya: craft two short email variants per persona and ship to SDR queue for pilot (ETA 2026-03-10).
- Diego: prepare the 5-minute demo template showing canary rollback and latency routing (ETA 2026-03-05).
- Priya: author the ML notebook for the eval quickstart (ETA 2026-03-17).

Notes to self: keep language metric-forward for backend/platform; behavior-forward (evals/rollback) for ML. Avoid generic "we're low-latency" claims — show numbers and replay demos.

Quick shareable snippets (copy-paste):
- "Can we run a 50-prompt eval on your workload and show expected token delta in 30 minutes?"
- "We can replay 15 minutes of traffic and demonstrate routing-based tail-fallbacks that keep P99 under your SLO."
- "Use the same API across hosted and private deployments — swap models without changing your app code."

Historical refs / context:
- Pulled insights from recent SRE war room postmortem (JIRA-STACK-919) and a Platform QBR note about quota sprawl. This doc is intentionally practical and short — use it as a script bank, not a final PRD.

End of notes.
